title: Workshop deployment primer: customer archetypes and hosting patterns
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight workshop notebook capturing the team discussion and recommended patterns for mapping customer POC workload archetypes to hosting choices (hosted, dedicated, private, and hybrid). The goal is to produce repeatable POC templates and a decision checklist we can hand to sales/solutions during scoping calls.

Attendees (informal):
- Priya N (SE lead)
- Miguel T (infra)
- Evelyn P (product-hosted-api)
- Samir P (solutions engineer)
- Jared L (customer success)

High-level goals from workshop:
- Distill 4 customer archetypes and 1 hybrid pattern that cover ~80% of incoming POC asks.
- Define minimal config for each (expected cost drivers, SLOs to validate, trace/metrics to collect).
- Capture failure modes and mitigations for quick decisioning.

Customer workload archetypes (definitions + signals to look for):
1) Rapid-prototyping SaaS feature (low data sensitivity)
   - Signals: short integration timeline, product team wants rapid iteration, public or non-sensitive input, focus on latency for in-product responses rather than strict throughput.
   - Typical ask: quick hosted API integration, short-term credits, want to test UX flows.

2) Predictable-high-throughput (batch embeddings / vectorization)
   - Signals: large corpus, periodic batch jobs, cost sensitivity, embeddings as primary output, throughput > latency.
   - Typical ask: cost-per-embedding analysis, throughput/cost SLA.

3) Regulated enterprise (PII / compliance / audit)
   - Signals: legal/infosec involvement early, need for VPC or on-prem deployment, strict audit/KMS requirements, longer procurement.
   - Typical ask: Private deployment with KMS, audit log retention, contract-level SLA.

4) Real-time low-latency edge/close-to-user
   - Signals: sub-100ms p95 requirement, geographic distribution, model quantization acceptable, possibility of local edge nodes.
   - Typical ask: dedicated pools with regional placement or private with edge nodes.

Hybrid pattern: Burst-capacity + Private baseline
   - Pattern: Customer wants private control plane + predictable baseline capacity but expects occasional bursts beyond committed capacity. We provision a private baseline (or dedicated) and configure routing/fallback to hosted model variants for bursts. Useful when procurement limits baseline commit but UX requires durability under spikes.

Decision matrix (quick checklist per POC):
- Data sensitivity: public | low | medium | high
- Latency target: interactive (<200ms) | near-realtime (200-500ms) | batch
- Throughput shape: steady | diurnal | spiky | batch-only
- Cost constraint: low | medium | high willingness to pay for SLOs
- Ops handshake: simple API vs network/VPN setup vs on-prem install
- Rollout complexity: single model vs multi-stage canary

Mapping archetypes -> recommended hosting option (short guidance):
- Rapid-prototyping SaaS -> Hosted API with caching and prefix reuse. Rationale: lowest time-to-value, instrument token-level cost metrics, encourage auto-batching suggestions. POC config: 1–2 hosted models, streaming enabled, KV-cache TTL for session reuse. Success metrics: product acceptance, p95 latency < 400ms, token cost per 1k tokens target.

- Predictable-high-throughput -> Dedicated reserved capacity or batch jobs via dedicated clusters. Rationale: better unit economics, predictable throughput. POC config: reserved GPU pool with autoscaling disabled for baseline and scheduled batch windows. Evaluate batching efficiency and token/sec metrics. Success metrics: cost per embedding, throughput sustained for 4-hour window, cache-hit-rate for duplicate docs.

- Regulated enterprise -> Private (VPC/on-prem) with KMS and audit hooks. Rationale: compliance, data locality, and isolation. POC config: private control plane, customer-managed networking, HSM/KMS integration, limited egress policies. Success metrics: pass security checklist, encryption-at-rest verification, audit log completeness.

- Real-time low-latency edge -> Dedicated regional pools or private + edge proxies. Rationale: local placement reduces RTT; quantized models reduce inference time. POC config: small regionally placed dedicated nodes, model quantization profile, local cache warmers. Success metrics: p95 < target, cold-start frequency, model quality delta post-quantization.

Tradeoffs and quick mitigations (captured from discussion):
- Hosted is fastest but may have cadence limits for data residency. Mitigation: use hosted for non-sensitive proofs and document migration path to private.
- Dedicated reduces cost variance but increases ops for scaling. Mitigation: provide pre-baked autoscaling policies and templates.
- Private gives compliance but lengthens procurement and on-boarding time. Mitigation: offer a pared-down POC image and managed deployment checklist to speed initial onboarding.
- Hybrid burst routing can leak data to hosted endpoints if not carefully gated. Mitigation: provide clear policy templates and opt-in consent with obfuscation options for burst traffic.

POC measurement plan (minimum required telemetry):
- p50/p95/p99 latency (tokens) per route
- tokens/sec, tokens-per-request distribution
- cost per 1k tokens and cost per 1M embeddings
- error rate and cause breakdown (timeouts, OOM, infra)
- cache hit rate and effective cache savings
- cold-start frequency and amortized cold-start cost

Acceptance criteria (example templates):
- Hosted prototype: product team validates UX, p95 < 400ms for interactive flows, sample quality pass rate >= 85% on small eval set.
- Dedicated throughput POC: sustain required throughput for 2x planned concurrency for 2 hours, cost target met within 10%.
- Private: security sign-off from customer infosec and baseline SLA met in staging environment.

Risks noted and suggested mitigations (short list):
- Model degradation after quantization -> run side-by-side A/B evals and maintain fallbacks to FP16 variant.
- Underestimated burst patterns -> simulate spikes with synthetic traffic early.
- Network egress and data leakage in hybrid bursts -> default to anonymization/obfuscation and document policy.

Operational checklists for the SE quickly deployable during scoping calls (copyable bullets):
- Confirm data sensitivity and required retention window.
- Ask for representative payload sizes and concurrency expectations.
- Request sample traffic patterns (CSV or simple JSON histogram).
- Agree on 3 acceptance criteria and one rollback condition.
- Share link to pre-approved POC templates and costs.

Concrete next steps (owners and rough ETA):
- Finalize 4 POC templates (hosted, dedicated, private, hybrid) and upload to SE playbook (owner: Priya N) - ETA 2025-01-20.
- Create infra templates for dedicated baseline + autoscaling presets (owner: Miguel T) - ETA 2025-01-27.
- Draft compliance checklist for Private POC (owner: Evelyn P) - ETA 2025-01-17.
- Sampling harness for burst testing (owner: Samir P) - ETA 2025-01-24.

Notes to self / open questions to resolve in follow up:
- What is the minimal legal language we can provide to customers to allow hybrid burst routing without long procurement? (Action: Jared to coordinate with legal).
- Should we ship a reduced-cost dedicated trial tier for POCs to accelerate buy-in? (Action: product/finance to evaluate).

Quick references and examples used in discussion:
- Small embedding job reference costs (spreadsheet) - see linked confluence page.
- Prior retail POC where hybrid fallback saved 37% of cost during Black Friday traffic - internal case study.

Bottom line (one-paragraph):
For the majority of POCs we should default to hosted for speed unless a clear compliance or throughput economics case emerges. When customers need predictable unit economics or compliance, recommend dedicated or private respectively and pair those recommendations with a short, prescriptive POC checklist (metrics to collect, acceptance criteria, and rollback plan). The hybrid burst pattern should be offered only with explicit consent and a clear policy to avoid inadvertent data exposure.

End of notes.
